title: Engrafting human cortical organoids - Nature Biotechnology
gist: Reporting on a Nature paper, Nature Biotechnology describes 'xenocortication', transplanting human cortical organoids into the cortical cavity of neonatal immunodeficient apallial mice. Grafts grew about 4.7-fold between 2 and 3 months and made up nearly 92% of combined cortical tissue volume.

insights.claim: Limited intracranial space and interactions with existing neural circuits restrict growth and integration of human cortical organoids transplanted into rodents.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Overcoming these constraints is the bottleneck for in vivo human brain-disease models.
insights.quote: limited intracranial space and interactions with existing neural circuits can restrict their growth and integration following transplantation into rodents

insights.claim: Kaganovsky and colleagues transplanted human iPSC-derived cortical organoids into the cortical cavity of neonatal immunodeficient 'apallial' mice, in which most of the neocortex and hippocampus had been genetically depleted.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Creating space by depleting host cortex is a design choice that could be reused for other human-tissue chimeras.
insights.quote: The authors transplanted human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical organoids

insights.claim: MRI showed the grafts grew approximately 4.7-fold between 2 and 3 months after transplantation and accounted for nearly 92% of the combined cortical tissue volume.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Graft dominance of cortical volume indicates unusually strong engraftment, relevant for disease modelling and drug-testing platforms.
insights.quote: the grafts grew approximately 4.7-fold between 2 and 3 months after transplantation and accounted for nearly 92% of the combined cortical tissue volume
